newsitem.title: USA: Arizona governor takes the stand in own defense.
newsitem.headline: Arizona governor takes the stand in own defense.

text.p: Arizona Gov. Fife Symington took the stand Thursday in his federal fraud trial and repeatedly denied he was guilty of any criminal wrongdoing in his former life as a developer.

In a calm voice, the embattled two-term governor admitted he made frequent mistakes in financial statements given to real estate lenders in the mid-1980s to early 1990s, but that he never intentionally mislead them.

The state's chief executive also told the jury the blame should be shouldered by his former accounting firm, charging that Coopers & Lybrand should have caught the many "errors or omissions" that can be found in the documents.
"That's what they were there for," said Symington in U.S. District Court. "I'm not an accountant."

It was the first day of testimony by the 51-year-old Republican, who faces 22 counts of fraud, attempted extortion and perjury. If convicted on even a single count, the two-term governor would be ousted from the job he has held since 1991 and could be sentenced to prison.
Prosecutors maintain that the then-developer lied about his finances in the mid-1980s to early 1990s to save his real estate empire from collapsing.

The government contends he made the false statements to various financial institutions, telling lenders different stories depending on whether he sought money for projects or relief from his commitments.

Additionally, the government alleges Symington used his political office in an attempt to extort six union pension funds into releasing him from a personal gaurantee on a $10 million loan. The loan was used to finance a Hispanic-themed shopping centre in downtown Phoenix.
He faces a charge of lying under oath for statements he made during a bankruptcy court proceeding. Symington filed for Chapter 7 in September 1995.
Under questioning from defence attorney John Dowd, Symington attempted to knock down the individual charges one-by-one during his nearly day-long testimony.
Symington meticulously reinforced the basic themes of his defence in his own words, fleshing out what has previously been an outline for the eight-man, eight-woman jury.
"I did not," he continually said when asked whether he tried to defraud lenders or extort money from the unions.
Symington explained away the differing financial statements, saying he failed to change the dates when he updated them for another financial institution later.
He also was taken through a series of documents to show that lenders knew of his financial position and that he made changes when he discovered some of the mistakes.
"The financial statements just weren't a big priority for me," he said. "I was really busy, on the go."
The governor said he did not pay much attention to details and stressed that his role was to get the projects "on time and on budget" without fail.
He bolstered his claims with a 12-minute video of the roughly dozen, sometimes glittering developments that now dot the landscape in and around the Phoenix metro area.
Symington is the fifth and final witness put on by the defence, in sharp contrast to the more than two months of testimony by federal prosecutors.
